title: Harder than stone
hook: some stones split and water gushes out, yet some hearts are harder (2:74)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cow, and your line, don't make it harder. Did you do one thing the plain way? The cow story ends with a verse about what happens to hearts. Day three hundred forty-two.

Somewhere in the dark of a limestone cave, you can hear it: water is dripping. It's coming through the rock: through the ceiling, through solid stone, a drop at a time. Slowly, those drops hang icicles of stone from the roof. Rock seems like the last thing that would let anything through. And yet. Al-Baqarah, verse seventy-four, looks at a rock like that, and then at a human heart. Today: harder than stone.
screen: `WATER DRIPPING IN THE DARK.` → `THROUGH SOLID STONE.` → `A ROCK, AND A HEART.`

segments.voice: The verse comes straight after the cow. The people had seen the sign, the dead man brought to life, as verse seventy-three puts it, and the verse says: then, even after that, your hearts hardened, and became like rocks, or even harder. Then it does something unexpected. It defends the rocks. Among rocks, it says, there are some from which rivers burst out. There are some that split open, and water comes out of them. And there are some that fall down out of awe of God. In other words, the comparison isn't fair to the stone. Stone gives way. Stone lets water through. These listeners had seen exactly that: a few verses earlier, Musa struck a rock and twelve springs gushed out. The Arabic for this hardening is qaswah, and the Qur'an uses the word for hearts in other surahs too. It isn't a heart that feels nothing. It's a heart that has seen and stopped responding. Muslim tradition doesn't treat that as permanent. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad tells of a man who complained to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that his heart had grown hard. The Prophet told him: if you want your heart to soften, feed the poor, and pass your hand over the head of an orphan. Not a lecture. Not a feeling to manufacture. Two small acts of tenderness, with the hands. The verse looks at rock and finds water in it. Even stone lets water through.
screen: `EVEN AFTER THAT, HEARTS HARDENED` · `THE VERSE DEFENDS THE ROCKS` · `QASWAH: SEEING, NOT RESPONDING` · `FEED THE POOR, TOUCH AN ORPHAN'S HEAD`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften toward one person. Think of someone you've gone hard toward. Not someone who harmed you badly; someone you've just stopped responding to. A sibling, a coworker, an old friend. Picture their face. Picture them on an ordinary day, tired, carrying something you can't see. Let one drop through. You don't have to fix anything. Just notice whether the stone gives a little. The bell holds the time.
Harder than stone. Al-Baqarah's picture of a heart that has seen and stopped responding, set beside rocks that split and let water out. Today's word.
Your line: even stone lets water through. Today, do one small kind thing with your hands for the person you thought of. Day three hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims who feel their hearts growing hard are often advised, following a hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad, to soften them through small acts of care: feeding the poor and showing tenderness to orphans.

fork.setup: a man tells the Prophet his heart has grown hard. what does the Prophet tell him?
options: pray all night until it softens.
feed the poor and pass your hand over an orphan's head.
fork.reveal: two small acts of tenderness, with the hands. the cure for a hard heart, in this hadith, is care for someone else.

original.note: Arabic: hardness of heart; in 2:74, hearts that hardened like rocks.

trapdoor: what you thought: hearts like stone, a simple insult.
what it means: a heart that has seen signs and stopped responding, set beside stones that still let water through.
what a scholar hears: 2:74 lists three kinds of rock, gushing, splitting, falling in awe, and the commentators note the echo of the rock that gave twelve springs in 2:60.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:72–73 (the slain man, brought to life)
Musnad Ahmad (a man complains of a hard heart; feed the poor, stroke the orphan's head)

notes: 2:74 is paraphrased throughout; Pickthall's wording was not quoted because the writer was not certain of it.
The hadith of the hard heart is in Musnad Ahmad (often numbered 7576 or 9018 depending on edition) and graded hasan by some; confirm number and grading.
The link between 2:74's rocks and 2:60's twelve springs is a commentators' observation; confirm it's stated in a classical tafsir.
'Stone lets water through' with the cave picture is a modern illustration, not from the commentaries.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Walk into...' and drops 'thousands of years'; 'the slain man's killer revealed' (commentary) replaced with 2:73's own words; 'again and again' and 'the hardest thing there is' cut.
